narrative:
Greenhouse.io engagement (2026-05-15): secret hunt only (bucket hunt blocked by policy). Three passes run — Pass A scanned the 'greenhouse' GitHub org (trufflehog), Pass B cloned three third-party repos found via code-search, Pass C ran noseyparker over those same repos. Total 66 candidates: 1 trufflehog-verified TrelloApiKey, 65 noseyparker-only hits. Ownership verification ran for the one actionable repo owner (Sahabalam) and returned 'unowned' cleanly.

What worked: the ownership-verifier pipeline performed exactly as intended. Sahabalam is an independent bug-bounty researcher whose 'bugbounty' repo contains a getwaymore.txt Wayback URL dump of app.interseller.io. The verifier correctly identified zero Greenhouse/Interseller affiliation: Check A returned 37 hits all in Sanskrit text corpora, Check B returned 0 hits across 3000 program-domain Wayback URLs (word_boundary mode active), Check C was structurally inapplicable (GitHub username, not a bucket). Verdict 'unowned' promoted correctly despite Check A's ambiguous total count — the note field gave the verifier enough evidence to conclude without a positive signal.

What did not work: Pass A (trufflehog github --org=greenhouse) consumed budget for zero verified secrets. Greenhouse is a mature, security-conscious SaaS company with an active bug-bounty program; their GitHub org appears to be well-scrubbed. Pass B's one code-search repo (Sahabalam/bugbounty) contained a Wayback URL dump that generated 65 noseyparker false-positives — api_key/apikey/access_token URL query parameters and Shopify Pay transaction tokens embedded in Wayback-crawled URLs, plus two Google API keys belonging to Mozilla Rally. None of these are Greenhouse or Interseller credentials. The single trufflehog-verified TrelloApiKey was also in this same dump, meaning the key was captured in an app.interseller.io Wayback URL — it belongs to whatever third party had Trello integration active at that URL at crawl time, not to Greenhouse itself.

What surprised us: the combination of a trufflehog-verified hit AND ownership=unowned in the same repo was a clean stress-test of the workflow gate. The Trello key is real and active (trufflehog verified it against the Trello API) but belongs to an independent researcher's captured data — not Greenhouse. Greenhouse's own policy explicitly states 'Leaked API keys due to a customer issues or mis-configuration will not be eligible for bounties,' which would cover this case even if ownership had been ambiguous.

Recommended pre-flight for next greenhouse engagement: skip Pass A entirely — the org has already proven clean and re-scanning it wastes trufflehog quota with zero return. Focus any new run on Pass B/C with tighter code-search queries scoped to interseller.io (the acquired product) rather than both base names. Consider adding a repo-owner denylist entry for Sahabalam since all 66 candidates in this run originated from that researcher's archive repos. If the TrelloApiKey is still verified-active on a future run, investigate whether it appears in any Greenhouse-controlled context before pursuing further.

Pass A on org 'greenhouse' returned 0 verified secrets consistent with H3 signal; however H3 specifies narrative note only (no hard rule) in v1 — the observation is captured in the narrative section above.
